Lives · 1888–1981

Robert Moses

Cities & Power · New York · 1888–1981

2 min read1 figure, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected 2 timesUpdated 21 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersWhere it is contestedCorrectedThe definitive biographyReads across to

He never won an election and never ran a city. For forty years he decided what New York would look like.

If you keep one line

Build the thing that funds itself and you never have to ask anyone again. That is the danger, not the trick.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Moses held no elected office worth the name. His power ran through public authorities, and the Triborough Bridge Authority was the machine. An authority funded by its own tolls needs no budget line, so it needs no legislature. Bond covenants pledged the state not to impair the bondholders' contracts, which left Moses answerable to bondholders rather than to voters — and a contract cannot be repealed by someone who never signed it. Surplus tolls had to be reinvested in new authority projects. The machine was therefore built to keep building.

What it produced is genuinely enormous, and the count everyone repeats is Caro's: public works costing $27 billion, among them the parkway and expressway network the region still runs on. It also cleared people. Caro puts the number displaced by highway construction alone at 250,000. For the Cross-Bronx Expressway, by his account, Moses took a line through 159 buildings holding 1,530 families rather than one through six buildings holding nineteen.

He was not voted out, because there was no election to lose. In March 1968 Nelson Rockefeller folded Triborough into the new Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which could at last spend the tolls on the subway — the one use Moses had always refused. He had standing to sue and chose not to, on a promise of a role that never arrived. He answered his critics in a typewritten statement two years later, raising his glass, in effect, to the builder who could clear a ghetto without moving anyone, and to the chef who could make an omelette without breaking eggs.

02Where it is contested

The most repeated fact about him may not be one. Caro reports that Moses had the Southern State Parkway bridges built too low for buses, keeping poor and Black New Yorkers off the road to Jones Beach. The source is Sidney Shapiro, an aide who talked on condition that nothing appear until he was dead; he died in 1972, and no written order has ever surfaced. Langdon Winner made the story the standard case that objects carry politics. Bernward Joerges then found that buses reached the beach by other routes and that the bridges' designer put the low clearances down to cost. Thomas Campanella measured twenty of them and found them markedly lower than those on comparable parkways. Kenneth Jackson says flatly that Caro is wrong; Thomas Bender says the revisionists let unaccountable power off too lightly.

03Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 9 · Sept 2026 · Six lives said more than their sources.

A sourcing pass opened the documents behind the figures in eight lives, and six said more than those documents do. Fritz Haber said roughly half the nitrogen in your body came through his process and that three to four billion people are alive because of it. The first line was found in no document opened. The study most often cited gives 48 per cent of the world's population in 2008, and the entry now says that. John D. Rockefeller put Standard Oil's ninety per cent of American refining in the early 1880s; the source opened puts it at 1879. Andrew Carnegie called the 1901 sale the largest transaction in industrial history; neither source opened says so, and the sentence now says what they do. Robert Moses gave thirteen bridges and hundreds of playgrounds as Caro's count; only the $27 billion was found. Steve Jobs said he paid Lucasfilm for its graphics group; by Alvy Ray Smith's account the new company paid for the technology out of Jobs's ten million. Tu Youyou's sixty laboratories are sixty institutions in the WHO's count. Each figure now carries the document it was read in.

№ 16 · Sept 2026 · Five quotations the house had not seen.

An audit of quotations checked each one against the document it comes from. Five could not be found in any document the house could open, so they are no longer printed in quotation marks: Confucius on not imposing on others (the translator was never named), Ibn Khaldun on dynasties lasting three generations (not found in the Rosenthal translation the entry relies on), Robert Moses's 'stein' statement (two wordings circulate, and the 1981 obituary that carries it could not be opened), Clair Patterson's 1966 testimony about the Public Health Service, and Thomas Blanton's line about Arkhipov. Each is now given as a paraphrase, which is what the colophon says an unquoted line is. None of them has been shown to be wrong. Separately, Tu Youyou's entry called Rao, Zhang and Li's book the only book-length account in English; Tu's own 2017 book covers the same discovery, as chemistry rather than history.

04The definitive biography

The Power Broker: Robert Moses and the Fall of New YorkRobert A. Caro · 1974

The book that made his reputation and then unmade it — still the best account anywhere of how unelected power actually assembles itself. Read it alongside Hilary Ballon and Kenneth T. Jackson's 'Robert Moses and the Modern City' (2007), which argues Caro overstated the man and understated the century he worked in.

05Reads across to

Water in the West — the same shape: a landmark polemic about infrastructure, and the historians who arrived afterwards with the qualifications.

Frances Perkins — the same insight about where power actually sits, turned toward protecting people rather than moving them.

Emily Warren Roebling — the same city and the opposite instinct about names: she worked under someone else's, he made sure everything carried his.
